paragraphs.text: EVODIUS, ON THE FAITH, AGAINST THE MANICHAEANS

There is one God, Father and Son and Holy Spirit: invisible, incomprehensible, ineffable, inviolable, incapable of being defiled, who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light. He is the true light, the life and the truth, good, supreme, and whatever else human speech can say of him; yet these things are given by him, so that he may in some way be spoken of. From him are all things, and through him are all things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and in him, as is made plain in both Testaments to those who seek humbly and devoutly. To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Mani says that God has an adversary, some prince or other of the race of darkness, whom he also claims is unbegotten and has no author by whom he was created. Now if he is unbegotten and not created, he is certainly immortal in his own right. And if he is immortal in his own right, God will not be the one who alone has immortality, and the Apostle, who says of God that he alone has immortality, will be a liar. But since the Apostle is not a liar, God alone has immortality. And so he alone can grant immortality to souls and to whatever bodies he wishes.

So Mani's claim that some nature or other of evil, together with its prince, has no author but is unbegotten is false. Further, if God is unbegotten and the race of darkness is unbegotten too, then unbegotten and unbegotten will not be opposites, nor seeing and seeing, reigning and reigning, living and living, eternal and eternal. And if evil is the opposite of good, the good will disagree with the evil in some respect; but in many respects they will be joined and in agreement, and it will no longer be pure evil, since it has so many goods in common with God. If they say, "It is unbegotten in its own way," they say nothing. For unbegotten and unbegotten, eternal and eternal: insofar as they are unbegotten and eternal, they were never opposites. Because an emperor is great in his power and a menial slave is contemptible in his work, does it follow that the slave is not a man because the emperor is a man?
But if anyone asks what evil is, let him hear the Apostle saying: "The root of all evils is greed; some who desired it have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows."

Greed in each person is not natural but voluntary, which is why he said, "some who desired it." For what is had by desiring would not be had if it were not desired. The Lord too, showing that it lies in a man's power, says: "Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad." And in the Acts written by Leucius, which they themselves accept, it is written: "For specious fictions and feigned display and the compulsion of visible things do not proceed from their own nature, but from man, who through himself has been made worse by seduction." Even Mani himself could not help admitting that souls, even those he says belong to God's substance, sin by their own will. For in the second book of the Treasury he says: "But those who through their own negligence have not allowed themselves to be cleansed of the stain of the aforesaid spirits, and have not fully obeyed the divine commandments, and have been unwilling to keep more completely the law given them by their liberator, and have not governed themselves as was fitting," and so on. Likewise in the Epistle of the Foundation he says of those souls: "Who, through love of the world, have allowed themselves to stray from their former shining nature, and have become enemies of the holy light, and have openly armed themselves for the destruction of the holy elements, and have obeyed the fiery spirit; who have also afflicted with their hostile persecution the holy church and the elect established in it, the keepers of the heavenly precepts: these are shut out from the blessedness and glory of the holy land. And because they have allowed themselves to be overcome by evil, they will remain in that same stock of evil, that peaceful land and the immortal regions being forbidden to them. This will befall them because they have so bound themselves by wicked works that they have been estranged from the life and freedom of the holy light. They cannot therefore be received into those peaceful kingdoms, but will be fastened into the aforesaid horrible globe, over which a guard must also be set. Hence these same souls will cling to the things they loved, left behind in that same globe of darkness, having earned this for themselves by their own deserts. For they did not take care to learn of these things to come, nor did they separate themselves from them when time was given."

I ask you: when you hear these words, do you still doubt that Mani was forced to admit that sin is a matter of one's own will? He did not say just one word to that effect, but so many that they would wake anyone, however deeply sunk in sleep. He said "through their own negligence"; he said "have not allowed"; he said "have not fully obeyed"; he said "have been unwilling to keep"; he also said "have obeyed"; he said "have allowed themselves to be overcome"; he said "have bound themselves"; he said "having earned this for themselves by their own deserts"; he said "for they did not take care to learn of these things to come, nor did they separate themselves from them when time was given." And you hesitate to say that sin is committed by one's own will?

Again he himself says in the same epistle: "But the leftover part of the light, that is, the sinful souls"—and you say that only the race of darkness sins? But why should I speak of him, who, though he was in error, nonetheless tried to say this out of the plainest truth, when you refuse to understand our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who says that fire has been prepared for sinners and for the devil and his angels, all of whom he meant to be understood as sinners? For there is no injustice with God, that he should condemn those who have committed no sin.

For what else is sinning but failing to stand firm in the precepts of truth, or in truth itself? If sinners do this without willing it, they are judged unjustly. And that angels too come under judgment the Apostle shows when he says: "Do you not know that we shall judge angels?" They would not come under the judgment by which they are judged unless they came under sin, by which they become guilty and can deservedly be judged. For righteous men are not going to judge righteous angels, whom they will resemble, but certainly sinful ones. Each person, then, is the author of his own wrongdoing through greed.

So whether greed exists lies within our power, and therefore evil too lies within our power. What lies within our power, then, is something that ought not to be in our will; for evil cannot be a nature or a substance or a life, because these are good insofar as they exist. And if we call some people evil by nature, we say so because of the origin in the ancient sin, in which our mortality is now born. Everything, then, that is called evil in human beings is either sin or punishment. Sin is committed by the rational soul, which has free choice of the will; and punishment is inflicted by the justice of God, which does nothing unjustly. Against this the Manichaeans bark with their usual blindness; and when they are proven wrong, and shown that evil is not a nature but that it lies in a person's power to do good or evil, they say that the soul has no free will, and they do not see their own blindness.

For who would not cry out that it is foolish to give commands to someone who is not free to do what is commanded, and unjust to condemn someone who had no power to fulfil what he was ordered? And these wretches do not understand that they are attributing such injustices and iniquities to God. But what is true, if not that the Lord gives commands, that souls have free will, that evil is not a nature but a turning away from God's commands, and that God's judgment, by which he condemns sinners, is just?

Meanwhile, although Mani says that God abounds in all goods, that nothing in his glorious kingdoms is lacking or placed in a lowly state, and that his most splendid ages are so firmly founded that they can never be shaken or moved by anyone, in another place a little later he adds and says: "But the Father of the most blessed light, knowing that a great ruin and devastation, which would rise from the darkness, threatened his holy ages unless he set against it some outstanding and glorious deity, mighty in power, by which he might at once overcome and destroy the stock of darkness, so that once it was extinguished, rest might be secured for the inhabitants of the light."

Surely, then, the kingdoms of Mani's god could never be shaken or moved by anyone. For if they could, he lied in saying that those kingdoms could not be shaken by anyone. And if they were shaken by necessity or fear, he who could be shaken in this way will not be God. For we see that, according to this same Mani, the god of Mani was pressed by the evil of necessity: since ruin and devastation threatened his ages and he had nothing else he could do, he gave up part of himself to the battle, so that in this way at least he might secure rest for the inhabitants of the light. And that very part of him—light from light, good from good, holy from holy, eternal from eternal, god from god, almighty from almighty—has been corrupted, put to death, and mixed through all the bodies of the world from the highest to the lowest, from heaven down to dung, so that even prostitutes in the theaters, and fouler ones in fouler places, hold within themselves an oppressed god who perhaps cannot be set free. For at the end of that very epistle, from which we have already quoted a chapter, he says that the part of God which has been mixed cannot be brought back in its entirety to its former freedom.

Behold the victory, behold the triumph that Mani's god achieved! For after losing part of himself he is in mourning, as the same Mani says, and he has a veil before him to temper his grief, so that he may not see the corruption of his part. For today the divine substance he speaks of lies subject to the race of darkness like clay to the potter. This is written in the first book of their Treasury.

And what foulness, too, he wrote in the seventh book of that same Treasury, among other foul things, saying: "Then that blessed Father, who has the shining ships as his lodgings and dwellings according to his greatnesses, in his innate clemency brings help by which his living substance is stripped free and released from its impious bonds and its straits and anguish. And so by his invisible nod he transfigures those powers of his which are kept in this most brilliant ship, and makes them appear to the opposing powers which are stationed in each of the regions of the heavens. And since these consist of both sexes, male and female, he orders the aforesaid powers to appear partly in the form of beardless boys to the opposite sex, the females, and partly in the form of shining virgins to the contrary sex, the males, knowing that all these hostile powers, because of the deadly and most filthy lust innate in them, are very easily captured and enslaved by these same most beautiful forms which appear to them, and in this way are dissolved. And you should know that this same blessed Father of ours is the very same thing as his powers, which for a necessary cause he transforms into the undefiled likeness of boys and virgins. He uses them as his own weapons, and through them he accomplishes his will."

"The shining ships are full of these divine powers, which are set against the infernal races in the manner of a marriage, and which with eagerness and ease accomplish whatever they have conceived in the same instant. So when reason requires that these holy powers appear to males, they at once display their likeness in the guise of most beautiful virgins. Again, when it comes to the females, they set aside the form of virgins and show the form of beardless boys. At this comely sight their ardor and lust increases, and in this way the bond of their most wicked thoughts is loosed, and the living soul which was held in their members, released on this occasion, escapes and is mingled with its own most pure air; there the souls, thoroughly washed, ascend to the shining ships, which have been prepared for their conveyance and for their passage across to their homeland."

"But that which still bears the stains of the opposing race comes down bit by bit through heat and warmth and is mingled with trees and the other plants and all crops, and is tinged with various colors. And in the same way that, from this great and most brilliant ship, figures of boys and virgins appear to the opposing powers which dwell in the heavens and have a fiery nature, and as a result of this comely sight the part of life held in their members is released and drawn down through the heat to the earth: in the same way also that most high power which dwells in the ship of the living waters appears, through its angels, in the likeness of boys and holy virgins to those powers whose nature is cold and moist and which are stationed in the heavens. To those of them who are female the form of boys appears, and to the males that of virgins. By this change and variety of divine and most beautiful persons, the princes of the moist and cold stock, male or female, are dissolved, and what is living in them flees; but what remains behind is released and drawn down into the earth through the cold, and is mixed with all the kinds of things on earth."

Who would not laugh, or rather grieve over and detest this man, who says such horrible and execrable things about the divine substance? So, according to your error and your doctrine, the substance of eternal light, the part of God that is in captivity, in calamities, in hardships, in oppression, in filth and uncleanness, could not be helped day by day in any other way than by the blessed Father, who has the shining ships as his lodgings and whom you call the Third Envoy, and the most high power changing their powers into the nature of the different sexes; powers which you indeed call undefiled, yet which, in the manner of prostitutes, by their beauty inflame the deadly and most filthy lust of the princes of darkness, each sex the other. For you have found no word by which you could ever express such foulness more decently. And why do they do this? So that, once the princes are stirred to lust, the divine substance may find an opportunity for release. What does this mean but that the divine majesty finds ways of escape even through the genitals of demons? Great God, come to the aid of the minds that believe such foulness and follow such abominations! Who would not shudder at these things, I ask you? Who is so blind as to believe them, I ask you?

But let those who follow Mani certainly answer me this: if God is incorruptible, or the whole nature of the highest good inviolable, unstainable, unapproachable, undefilable, incomprehensible, what could the nature of evil have done to so great a nature if he had refused to fight with it, so as not to be brought to such disgrace? This is what I asked: what would the race of darkness have done to God if he had refused to fight with it? If I am told "nothing," I ask why his part, that is, God of God, is today placed in calamities, in oppression, in captivity, in subjection, so that it is even set free so shamefully, and cannot be set free entirely even so; and why the Father himself is in mourning on account of that part of himself, a mourning that Mani proclaims most openly in his books.

Someone said: "Nothing could have been done to him; but he fought in order to show that he had foreknowledge of the thoughts of the princes of darkness, and to demonstrate that he feared nothing." To him I said: "He who could see the thoughts of the princes of darkness and feared no one, why did he not see the mourning that awaited him from the misfortune of his part, which he suffers today?" That part of his he will never recover entire, for something of it remains, as Mani himself says, which cannot be purified and will be condemned forever in the globe of darkness. A great foreknowledge, or rather ignorance and wretched weakness—that is all his fearing no one amounts to. Surely, if he could not protect himself in any way, he should have begged to be spared, so that that integrity and glory of all adornments would not be brought to such disgrace.

Likewise someone said: "The race of darkness could do nothing to him, but he himself would not tolerate an evil thing near his borders, and he sent someone to subdue it." To him I said: "If it is as you say, then he himself turns out to be the evil one, since he wanted to destroy a neighboring thing that did him no harm. And just as he was evil toward that thing, so he was cruel toward his own part, or else ignorant of the calamity that would befall it. For when he thought he could achieve something good by extending his territory into the kingdom of evil, which was doing him no harm, he did not foresee, first, the misfortune that daily oppresses that part of his, and second, that he will never be able to bring it back entire to its former freedom."

But since no answer at all can be given to this objection, they put forward their usual ignorant reply: "What would the Jews have done to Christ if he had not been willing to suffer at their hands?" Oh, if only they could see—as they easily would, if they were not blinded by the fog of contentiousness—what it means to be pressed by the necessity of an impending evil, which they insist their god suffered; and what the most kindly office of mercy is, which the Lord Jesus Christ, the wisdom and power of God, by his will and his ineffable power, deigned to show to the human race through the man he took from the Virgin, so that through a man he might show men an example of patience. For it was fitting, and it was just, that human beings should overcome the difficulty of their weak flesh through humble patience, since they had fallen into it through proud self-exaltation, as our Scripture shows in Adam, the first man. Can you too say that, because there were some people whom God wished to teach patience, he chose to suffer such great evils at the hands of the race of darkness, as the Lord did at the hands of the Jews? Or can you say that God took on some passible nature in which he might suffer whatever the race of darkness could do to him, while he himself remained in no way changed in his own substance—just as the Word of God, who is the Son of God and is himself unchangeable like the Father, took on a mortal man, so that, with his divinity whole and inviolate, he might in mortal flesh teach mortals to conquer death through patience, and might show by the resurrection the future change of that weak flesh for the better?

So, though invisible in himself, he appeared visible in the man whom he deigned to take from a woman, as we read in the Gospel. The Apostle too says, "born of a woman." And these people say: "Why did he not say 'of a virgin'?" They do not understand that this was said in the customary way, according to the particular usage of the language of the Scriptures, just as it was said of Eve, "He formed her into a woman," even before she had been presented to the man. Mary, however, is not inappropriately called a woman because she gave birth, and a virgin because she knew no union with a man and her virginity was not violated by giving birth. As for the angel and Elizabeth saying to Mary, "Blessed are you among women," there is no difficulty, for truly the Virgin is blessed among women. But do not say: "He had a body in the way the angels appeared, so as not to be born of a woman." What then? If you were asked, "Where have you read that Christ came in the flesh?" would you not answer, "In the Gospel"? Then the reply to you is that it is written there that Christ was born of a virgin. But with your usual foulness you will say that this very passage of Scripture is false. Nor do you see that someone as blind as you can do the same thing: say that what you call true is false, and that what you call false is true. And so you would open the doors to every human error and crime, so that each person might accept the divine Scriptures themselves just as he pleased or as it delighted him, and reject whatever, not understanding and taking offense, he considered bad; and no rule would be found by which such errors as yours could be corrected.

Accept the canonical Scriptures whole, if you wish to be whole yourselves. For if you understood, or at least believed, what the Apostle said—that our race was deceived through a woman, for he says, "I fear lest, as the serpent seduced Eve by his cunning, so your minds too may be corrupted"—you could understand that our race had to be set free through a woman, so that, since death came about through a woman, life might be recovered through a woman, and so it might be shown that it is not the female creature itself that is to be blamed, of which God is the maker, but the will by which Eve sinned. But they are afraid to believe that the undefilable and ineffable power of that majesty was in a virgin's womb, lest it be polluted by her blood; yet he has dwelt and now dwells in the apostles and in many worthy women, who certainly have bodies and have blood. For if he could be defiled in Mary, he could be defiled in all of them; but if he could not be in them, then certainly he could not be in Mary either, in whose womb the wisdom of God brought about the taking up of a body.

They will certainly not deny that Mani himself was born of a father and a mother. Nor, likewise, will they deny that by their error his soul is God almighty. With astonishing pride he boasts that he was taken up by his twin, that is, by the Holy Spirit. And surely, if he is the twin of the Holy Spirit, he too is the Holy Spirit, and he too is God almighty, as the Holy Spirit is. Yet this Mani had flesh. If the Holy Spirit, or Mani's soul, the twin of the Holy Spirit, was defiled in that flesh, then they worship a God who can be defiled. But God is nowhere defiled. Even the light of the heavenly bodies reaches down to the earth and is not defiled, and it is plain that this sun, to which they bend the knee, spreads its rays over all dung and stench and is nowhere defiled. Since that is so, let them stop blaspheming and pray God to free them from their error. For an undefilable substance is not undefiled because it touches nothing, but because it remains in its own purity, whatever it may touch. Take a body that is invulnerable or impenetrable: do we call it that because it is never struck by iron, or rather because even when it is struck it is not pierced? So the very fact that the Son of God was born through a woman proves all the more that he could not be defiled by a woman's blood. If he had not been born through a woman and had avoided those members, he would have seemed to show that he could be polluted by them, and we would call him undefilable with less confidence. Moreover, he consecrated virginity, because he willed to be born of a virgin. He needed only a mother on earth to be chosen so that he could take up humanity, since he already had a Father in heaven.

But they say: "Why then did he disown his mother when he said to her, 'Woman, what have I to do with you?' And why, when he was told that she wished to see him, did he answer, 'Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?' and count instead as his kin those who do the will of his Father?" It was because by his own example he was already teaching that earthly parents must be renounced for God's sake. Earthly affection ought not to clamor against one who is doing divine works. If he had no mother because he disowned his mother, then neither did Peter and the other apostles have fathers, since he admonished them, saying: "And call no one on earth your father; for you have one Father, who is in heaven." So what he admonished them to do about an earthly father, he did first himself about his mother. This, then, is what we say: the Wisdom of God was not defiled by taking up humanity. In mercy it took up a man for the salvation of humankind, so that, as the apostle says, he might become the mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ. He who said, "I am the truth," could not lie to his doubting disciple when he offered him the scars of his wounds, even for him to touch with his hand. If he had lied in this way to his own disciple, how could we trust him with confidence in anything? Far be such blasphemy! And may it not hold guilty forever those who dare to assert or believe it. May they wake up at last and understand how wicked and perverse it is to believe such things.

We, however, believe that Christ the Lord took up a true man. In him the invisible appeared visibly to men; in him he lived among men; in him he endured human things at the hands of men; in him he taught men what to turn away from, what to endure, and where to strive to go. Yet he did all this under no necessity. Hence he himself says: "For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life so that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again." So he did not lose his life through the necessity of evil. He willed that everything done in his passion should be done to teach human nature, not to protect his own. Consider how it is with us, who are made of soul and body, invisible as to the soul but visible as to the body. Whatever we receive visibly, whether honors and benefits or insults and injuries, we must refer to the soul, which is invisible, as to our ruler, since the soul rules the body. Indeed, although we are immortal as to the soul, when we have died in the body we are said to be dead. In the same way the Lord, as to the flesh and the form of a servant which he deigned to take up, is shown to have suffered insults and chains and scourges, and to have died. So we are to believe that the Truth did everything truthfully and nothing falsely. For by his power and will the Word was made flesh, and was born, suffered, died and rose again, under no necessity of his own but by will and power. No part of him was ever plundered, and no part is held captive even now: not only of his divinity, but not even of the mortal nature he took up. Nor can it ever be captured, except by those who wish to be joined to him through faith with a pure heart. He is not like the god of Mani, who is oppressed by the evil of necessity and even today, in part (as they cannot deny), wallows here in miseries and calamities.

Understand, if you can, how great the difference is between necessity and will, even among human beings. Suppose, for example, that someone is sent to prison by order of justice for what his sin deserved, and that another man, a holy man, enters that same prison to console him or set him free. Have both been placed in prison for the same reason? The one was sent, the other went in. The one suffers punishment, the other shows mercy. The one went in when he wished and came out when he wished; the other has no right to be freed unless a pardon intervenes. Human beings can do this, and they bestow such a kindness freely, sometimes when they want nothing in return. Consider, then, whether God can suffer any necessity, when even human beings can do good by their will, hired by no reward and compelled by no necessity. God therefore suffers no necessity, and what he does he does not by necessity, but by his supreme and ineffable will and power.

And yet you of all people, given your error, ought not to have raised the objection you make when you say: "What could the Jews have done to Christ if he did not wish to suffer at their hands?" For according to the blasphemies of that same Mani, Christ had no flesh and suffered nothing from the Jews. This is what he says in the Letter of the Foundation: "The enemy who hoped he had crucified that same Savior, the Father of the righteous, was himself crucified, for at that time one thing was done and another was shown. So it was the prince of darkness who was fixed to the cross. He, with his companions, wore the crown of thorns and had the scarlet robe. He also drank the vinegar and gall which some have supposed the Lord drank. And everything that he appeared to endure here was inflicted on the leaders of darkness, who were also wounded with the nails and the lance."

Why then do you object, saying, "What could the Jews have done to Christ if he did not wish to suffer at their hands?" when this is what you think of his passion: that God himself suffered nothing in his body, and that the prince of darkness suffered all those things? How can you raise this objection against our faith?

For we believe, as is written in the gospel, that Christ willed to suffer, and that he suffered when he willed. The Jews did not bring about the passion itself when they willed. They did indeed want to seize him and kill him, and in their will they had already accomplished the crime they were attempting. They were already guilty of a most monstrous sin because they willed it, even if they had done nothing. Yet he who had power to lay down his life allowed them to act when he willed. He could have commanded legions of angels to destroy the Jews, or slain them all with a single word.

So Christ the Lord suffered according to the man he took up. And no member of him is held by the Jews today, not even of the mortal body he had taken up, as we said above. But your god, O Manichaeans, was overwhelmed by impending ruin and devastation. He did not go out to battle of his own free will but was compelled by necessity. He did not wish to bestow anything; he was trying to resist. He was devoured and mixed in his own substance, not in a mortal body that he had taken up. Part of him is held captive today, and part will be held forever in the globe. And yet who could bear the incredible blasphemies these people do not hesitate to utter about the Lord's passion itself?

All the apostles and all rational tongues proclaim that Christ the Lord suffered. All sound faith confesses that Christ suffered for us. Yet Mani asserts that demons endured all those sufferings. He does not say they suffered because the Lord triumphed over them and taught us to triumph over them through patience. He says it because they deny that Christ the Lord had mortal flesh. To them we say: if he did not have mortal flesh, what was it that the Jews seized? What was it that hung on the cross? What was fastened with nails to the wood? What was pierced with the lance, so that blood and water flowed out? If these things only seemed to happen and did not really happen, they will be a phantom, and that it is wicked to believe.

But suppose they truly happened, yet not in mortal flesh, and you say they happened in the divine substance itself. Then you are saying that the divine substance is changeable, visible to fleshly eyes, tangible to fleshly hands, and vulnerable to iron, and that too it is wicked to believe. Mani was afraid to say that these things did not happen, and afraid again to say that they happened in the divine substance. He was also unwilling to confess, because he could not even understand, how the Son of God, through whom all things were made, took up a man with flesh without any change or defilement of his divine substance. So he was forced to say that it was not Christ but the prince of darkness with his companions who suffered all those things. Wretched people! Do you not fear that at the judgment it will be said to you: "I set free those for whom I suffered. Go! Let him set you free to whom you ascribe my sufferings"?

You say, in great error but you say it all the same, that Christ is born every day, suffers every day, and dies every day. In those, perhaps, who believe and who suffer tribulations and death for his name? "No," they say, "but in gourds and leeks and purslane and other things of that kind." What great absurdity, what great blindness! Earlier, people were freed from their sins by the sufferings of demons; here, by the sufferings of vegetables.

Again, when we say to them, "What could the race of darkness have done to God if he had not wished to fight with it?", they say: "Nothing could be done to an incorruptible God. If, for example, someone wanted to tear a solid glass sphere with his nails, the fury of his nails would never do anything to it." But if they even imagined the divine substance to be such that all the fury of the race of darkness was to it as a scratcher's nails are to a glass sphere, then the god of the Manichaeans would not be grieving today over a part of himself that was cut off and lost. They say that this part, when it is in fruits or plants, that is, in a melon or a beet or such things, knows its beginning, middle and end, but when it comes into flesh it loses all understanding. They say that a teacher was sent to human beings because the part of God has become foolish in them, and that one was not sent to melons because melons have a wise soul.

Who would believe that such things could ever be said by human beings, or among them? But how can you say that the substance of your god suffers no evil, when it is bound in fruits and blinded in flesh, or when it wishes to return and is cast down to earth by the race of darkness? If no evil has befallen or befalls it, then everything Mani said is false: in the Letter of the Foundation, which is the head of all vain fables; in the Treasure, which is a treasury of every obscenity and blasphemy; and in all his other books. In them, with endless talk, he asserts nothing but the misery of God's substance, which he says is mixed with the princes of darkness, and the sorrow of the divine powers in their great anxiety to set it free. In truth, the substance of God neither could nor ever can suffer any evil. Nor does it have any enemy to corrupt an unbegotten part of it. It is human beings who are enemies of God, or rather of themselves, when they do not obey God's commands and when by their desires they corrupt themselves, not God.

If you were willing to look at the harmony of the two testaments with a single eye, O Manichaeans, you would see it very easily. You rush rabidly at what is written: "The Spirit of God was borne over the water," and "God saw that it was good," and "Adam, where are you?" and "a jealous God," and "a devouring fire," and "my sword," and other such things. You do not consider that someone else might be blind enough to want to criticize what the Lord said in the gospel: "You shall not swear by heaven, for it is God's throne, nor by the earth, for it is his footstool." Such a person might say what you, with astonishing madness, are accustomed to say: "Where was God before heaven and earth existed?" Or he might attack what is written: "And Jesus marveled," since no one usually marvels except at something he did not know. (Seeing that something was good, by contrast, is no mark of ignorance; it means that what he had made pleased him.) Or he might attack what is written where the Lord says, "Who touched me?" and about Lazarus, "Where have you laid him?" and "I came not to send peace on earth but a sword," and "I came to cast fire into the world," and "I came so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind," and "Sell your possessions and buy yourselves swords"; or what the apostle says: "I am jealous for you with the jealousy of God," and "The wrath of God will be revealed from heaven against all ungodliness." There are countless other things said or done by the Lord himself or by the apostles which people who do not understand them could attack most insanely. The greedy or the depraved could also take in the wrong sense what the Lord said: that whoever has given up what he has will receive sevenfold or even a hundredfold in this age. Someone might want to give up a wife, a maidservant, or even prostitutes for the Lord's sake, and do it in hope of that multiplication, not out of love of righteousness. People who understand wrongly could also be horrified at his saying: "Unless one eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in him." And there is his saying: "Whoever says to his brother, 'Fool,' will be liable to the fire of Gehenna." Suppose fools were to say: "Look, the one you call merciful, who forgives sins, threatens Gehenna for an insult!" Would they not show that they have no idea where their own heads are, while thinking they are saying something clever? Or they might object that he handed over so many souls to be killed by demons in the swine, when you say that the souls of swine are like those of human beings. Or that with a word he withered the tree on which he found no fruit, because it was not the season, a tree you say has an intelligent soul.

See how much utterly wicked and blind people could say against the divine words, just as you, in ignorance, rush at the things done or said mystically in the old books and rashly accuse what you do not understand. Yet when things like these from the New Testament are put to you, you say they signify divine and spiritual things. You deny that the holy writings of the Old Testament can be taken figuratively, even though the Lord himself drew certain things from them in a figurative sense, and the apostle Paul writes that all things happened to that people as a figure. He himself showed the rule and expounded many things from those books. But perhaps, with your usual vanity and dull heart, speaking against the authority of the Lord or of the apostle, you say that the sayings of the Old Testament cannot be expounded at all, and that only the New can be expounded in such matters. You do not consider that you would have nothing to say if other impious people told you that it is rather the Old that can be expounded and the New that cannot. A sound mind, considering both testaments, will without doubt find in the one whatever it finds in the other that admits of exposition. Your inexperience, or rather your malice, is very plain. Look at the Acts of Leucius, which he writes under the name of the apostles, and see what kind of things you accept there about Maximilla, the wife of Egetes. She was unwilling to render her husband his due, although the apostle has said: "Let the husband render his due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband." So she substituted her maidservant, named Euclia, for herself with her husband. As it is written there, she adorned her with [?] enticements and cosmetics and put her in her place at night as her substitute, so that he, unaware, lay with her as if with his wife. It is also written there that when this same Maximilla and Iphidamia had gone together to hear the apostle Andrew, a certain handsome little boy, whom Leucius wants us to understand as God, or at least an angel, commended them to the apostle Andrew. Then he went on to the praetorium of Egetes, entered their bedchamber, and imitated a woman's voice, as if Maximilla were complaining about the pains of the female sex and Iphidamia were answering her. When Egetes heard these conversations, he believed the women were there and went away. What do you say to this, I ask you? Why did Maximilla not fear to bind souls in flesh by the utterly shameful procuring of her maidservant? And since you believe that this boy lied so shamefully, who would believe you when you speak, since when you lie you claim to be imitating the Lord?

But you, full of rashness, still rush at the old books, working harder to accuse what you do not know than to learn it. Consider what miracles are there, if you delight in the miracles of the New Testament. There the dead were first raised, there lepers were first cleansed, and there are many other things which become known to those who seek diligently and devoutly, and which build up faith. If you delight in good precepts, it was there that those two commandments were first written, about loving God and neighbor, which the Lord praises so highly. There we are told to leave home, parents, children and everything else for the Lord's sake; there, not to return evil for evil; there, to pray for our enemies; there, to forgive an enemy; there, to offer the cheek to be slapped. Whatever precepts are in the New Testament were not only commanded there but also fulfilled by holy men with all vigilance. Can your malice say this too: that whatever good and magnificent things are written there are false and were added later, while only those things which you think evil because you do not understand them are true? You ought to notice that other impious people could do the same with the New Testament. They could criticize whatever is there that they thought evil because they did not understand it, and say that these things alone are true. And they could say that everything openly glorified there is false and was added by lovers of the Lord, so that not everything in it would seem worth shunning. Then both you and they, struck with such blindness, already judged and condemned, would be shunned. Wake up at last and stop your blasphemies. If you intend to be Christians, accept the authority of all the holy canonical scriptures. Do not accuse what you do not understand, but rather desire to understand it.

And what of the fact that you deny the resurrection of the flesh? The apostle Paul cries out: "It is sown in corruption, it rises in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it rises in glory; it is sown in weakness, it rises in power; it is sown a natural body, it rises a spiritual body." And you shout back against him that human flesh cannot rise again and that its author is the prince of darkness, although the apostle says that this same flesh is the members of Christ and the temple of the Holy Spirit. "Do you not know," he says, "that your bodies are members of Christ?" He surely does not say this with regard to the weakness of our present corruption, which comes down from the penalty of original sin, but with regard to the adoption of the future resurrection. As he also says elsewhere: "And we ourselves groan within ourselves as we await the adoption, the redemption of our body." Elsewhere too, speaking of marriage, he compared this same flesh to the church, saying: "For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church." So when he says in another place, "The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh," he does not condemn the flesh so that we should regard it as an enemy. Rather, he urges us to bring it under our control, so that like a wife it may serve the spirit in conceiving and bringing forth good works. And this, he says, cannot happen except by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. For it is not the nature of the flesh that struggles against us but its penalty, because by sin we deserved to be mortal. Again he says: "Your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit within you." And yet, although this flesh is called grass because of its present weakness, you believe that John made gold out of grass, and you do not believe that almighty God can make a spiritual body out of a natural body. God is going to change the flesh and make a heavenly body out of it, when we shall be equal to the angels of God. Because of this change, the same apostle says most truly: "Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God."

But it is no wonder that you are so blind as to think these things cannot be done by almighty God, since you even say that God could not have made the world, or anything that has been made, except under a great and wretched necessity, and only because there was matter to help him in making the world, so that he could free his own part from it. Choose now, then, which you wish to follow. Will you follow a god who is less than powerful and weak, who, under the necessity of his own part being set in misery, was helped to make the world by matter he had not made himself? Or will you follow the almighty God, who under no necessity, but by his own will and supreme power, spoke and they were made, commanded and they were created; who calls the things that are not as though they were?

You, then, who have been deceived by this impiety of Mani, flee, make haste while you may, so that you do not earn eternal condemnation from that just Judge. Repent of your sins, if you wish to be set free, and do not listen to the Manichees when they say, "We do not sin, that is, the souls of light do not sin; it is the race of darkness that sins." For if that is so, why do they frighten us into believing them? They cannot say that unbelief is not a sin, since it is written: "Whoever does not believe is already judged."

If, then, unbelief is a sin, and only the race of darkness sins, it follows that the part of light is found free of all sin. All of them, then, return to the kingdom, because they do not sin, and no soul has anything to fear, because no soul sins at all. And what Mani says is false: that the cut-off portion of light, that is, the sinful souls, is condemned to guard the globe, so that some security may at long last be won for the divine kingdoms that were placed in danger. So either the part of light must sin, or the part of darkness. But if the part of light sins, God sins, which it is wicked to say. If the part of darkness sins, then it is called to the kingdom by him who said, "I have not come to call the righteous but sinners, because it is not the healthy who need a doctor, but those who are sick." Meanwhile that divinity from divinity, that light from light, degenerates and is joined forever to the race of darkness.

What a detestable error of mind in those who believe such things! Yet I wish you would pay attention and be willing to see that the one you say is by nature the supreme evil cannot possibly be evil. For if whatever he does, he does in such a way that he cannot depart from his nature and act otherwise, he does not sin at all; and if he does not sin at all, he does nothing evil; and so, if he has done nothing evil, he is certainly not evil. It follows, then, that the part of God, which is understood to be God, and which you call the soul, is alone guilty of all sins, and that you heap onto your own god everything you most insanely think deserves blame. But what does the truth proclaim? That a body, when it is lifeless, cannot sin, though sin can be committed through it; that an irrational soul cannot sin either, because it can neither receive the commands of reason nor attain happiness, but keeps, in its own rank, the order of nature that it has received; but that a rational soul, because it can grasp the reasonable commands for right action and by right action attain eternal happiness, is justly condemned to lower things if by sinning it refuses to do so, since nothing separates it from God except a perverse will.

Read this, Manichees, and examine it with all vigilance; read and examine it more and more, but with a fair mind, not a hostile one. Read it with attention, for at the coming judgement this writing will be a witness against you if, recognizing that what has been said is true, you do not hasten with all speed to the bosom of mother Church, the Catholic Church, which alone teaches the truth.

Judge at last, Manichees, and choose whom you wish to follow. Will it be the Father unbegotten, the Son only-begotten, and the Holy Spirit shared in the unity of the Father and the Son: one God, almighty, incorruptible, inaccessible, unchangeable, eternal, good, holy, merciful, just; who has no parts, because he is one, and no particle of whom can be separated from him, because he is inseparable; nothing of whom can be changed, because he is wholly unchangeable; nothing of whose substance can be corrupted even slightly [?], because he is wholly incorruptible; who willed, and all things were made, whatever exists, whatever lives, whatever understands (for he is himself the supreme substance, the supreme life, the supreme truth); who commanded, and all things were set in order, good in their own places and times; who saw fit to set the rational creation over all the rest of creation; and who, when that creation fell away from his laws by its own will through pride and went after visible things, mercifully saw fit to speak to it through his ministers and through himself, visibly showing it certain signs, examples and commands by which it might rise again and be restored [?] to eternal life? This is the God whom the Catholic faith proclaims.

Or will it be that god who is falsely called incorrupt, since he is afterwards found to be oppressed by the necessity of evil; fearful, since he was driven to war by the threat of ruin and devastation; full of ignorance, if he could not see what might happen to his part; cruel, if he foresaw the future misery of his part and, though he could have rested secure with it, still sent it into a wretched battle; evil, if, though nothing could be done to him by the nature of evil, he nevertheless tried to destroy it himself; reckless, since he dared to engage with that by which his part would be held captive and stained forever; changeable, since he has already been partly changed; corruptible, since he has already been partly corrupted; partly whoring, partly lying, partly blaspheming, partly committing every crime, since he is partly mingled with all these things; mourning, covered with a veil of mourning; subject to demons as clay to the potter, and brought by necessity even to a shameful role, so that, transformed into boys and girls, he might inflame the lust of the demons? This is the god whom Mani proclaims. Or else, if your conscience can, let it deny these things, with the true and eternal God as your witness, who will judge all: deny to yourselves even one of them.

But if what we say is true, look back at last, see at last in what death you are lying. Be humble, if you wish to be set free, and do not say proudly and impiously that you yourselves are almighty God. For that is what you are saying when you insist that your souls are parts of him, since God is not greater in one part and lesser in another. Rather, say to yourselves: God is unchangeable, we are changeable; God is incorruptible, we are corrupted by our desires; God cannot be defiled, we are defiled by our sins; God is wisdom itself, we are foolish and strive to attain wisdom; God is eternal and blessed life itself, we are wretched because of our sins and long to become blessed. Therefore we are not part of his substance. For if you are his parts and suffer so much, it follows that he too already suffers all these things in part, and could have suffered still more, as befell his part, had he not provided for himself through your misery. See, then, what you are. If you are his parts, you are God; if you are begotten by him, you are likewise God. Why then are you defiled by such corruption of sins? But if you were made by him, confess it, and you will no longer be Manichees.

49. For Mani says there are two natures, one good and the other evil: the good, which made the world; the evil, from which the world was made. But if God made us, Mani cannot find what God made us from. For if he made you from himself, you are what he is, and so you ought not to be defiled by such corruption of sins, as has already been said. If he made you from something alien, you do not belong to him, because he made you in the same way as the world. But if he made you neither from himself nor from something alien, but simply willed it by his omnipotence and you were made, then say so to Mani and renounce his error. For this is how it befits the Almighty to make what he wills, as the Catholic Church says: "He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created." Say to yourselves: We are not his parts, but his works. Say to yourselves: If God suffered under necessity and could not escape except by suffering the loss of his part, who will ever be able to be freed from such necessities? Or who will there be to protect a God who cannot protect himself? Or when will he be able to free me from this necessity of captivity, who could not keep me safe in his kingdoms while they were intact? For he did not send me out from there because I had sinned, but sent me out into sins themselves. Or when will he be able to help me, wretchedly placed in alien territory, who, to help himself, gave me over to such ruin so that he would not have to fight? If God himself is incorruptible, what would that nature of evil have done to him if he had refused to fight with it, so that I would not now be tormented like this? Or what injustice is this, that I should be condemned to the globe, and that I should endure so much here so that he may now be a little more secure? Surely, since I too am what he is, since I am his part, and no one in his kingdoms is set higher or lower [?], let us take turns suffering this misery, so that I too may rest a little and those kingdoms may be at peace without danger. And yet it is to be feared that this nature of evil cannot be kept in custody even when shut up in the globe. For if it corrupted incorrupt kingdoms and violated the inviolable substance of God, how is that part of light, that is, the sinful souls, which, vitiated, weak and feeble, are fixed in the globe to guard it, not swallowed up by it, so that, with no one now able to resist, it throws those divine kingdoms into total turmoil once more? Who would now dare to go out to war, when the part that went out was treated so unjustly that, with no rest for it [?], its own fellow citizens were condemned to guard the globe forever? Or if it cannot break through the globe to reach that bright covering of condemned souls, what need is there for it to be covered over by the condemnation of divine members? But if it can break through the globe, who, already wounded, will resist the one who wounded them when they were whole? Far be such grave and abominable blasphemy! Do not let this wickedness into your ears; do not entangle yourselves in so deadly a business. Flee Mani, and fly with all your longing to the breasts of Catholic truth.
